newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss envoy to US quits over Holocaust row.
newsitem.headline: Swiss envoy to US quits over Holocaust row.

text.p: Switzerland's ambassador to the United States resigned on Monday after a confidential document he wrote calling for "waging war" against Jewish groups and other critics was leaked to the press and triggered uproar.

In a letter released by the foreign ministry, Carlo Jagmetti said he was quitting because "I no longer find it appropriate to continue my activity as ambassador in this country until the retirement date of July 31, 1997 originally envisioned".
Switzerland's strained ties with Jewish organisations seeking compensation for Holocaust victims worsened with publication of excerpts from the leaked document on Sunday.

Swiss Jewish leaders had called for Jagmetti's ouster and slammed the comments, which came from a private strategy paper the envoy sent to Berne last month on how to handle a row over dormant accounts in Swiss banks of Hitler's victims.

"The leak, the resulting stories in the media and the reaction that followed from persons affected and from the public have created an intolerable situation for me," wrote Jagmetti, 64, who has been a Swiss diplomat more than three decades.

"What especially moves me is the accusation that the report reflects anti-Semitism," he wrote, insisting the remarks were taken out of context from a report that was never supposed to be published and expressing regret that he had caused offence.
Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti told reporters in Berne that the cabinet had accepted Jagmetti's resignation and would ask prosecutors to investigate the leak, the SDA news agency said.

It was a shame a distinguished diplomat's career had ended in such a way, Cotti said, but he added the paper's martial tone did not fit with the cabinet's aim to conduct an open dialogue with interested parties, especially the Jewish community.

"This is a war that Switzerland must wage and win on the foreign and domestic front," said Jagmetti's document, excerpts of which first appeared in the SonntagsZeitung weekly. "You cannot trust most of the adversaries," it said.

SonntagsZeitung said the "adversaries" to whom Jagmetti referred were Jewish groups and U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, who have accused the Swiss of profiting cynically from the war and are seeking compensation for Holocaust victims.
Swiss Jews were appalled by the tone of the document.
"I was shocked to see the insensitivity with which this matter is being addressed," said Thomas Lyssy, vice-president of the Swiss Jewish Federation (SIG).

The story broke a day after the biggest coalition party, the Social Democrats, demanded Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz resign for accusing Jewish groups last month of "blackmail" for demanding compensation for wartime suffering.

Delamuraz has since apologised for the remark, made in a newspaper interview as he finished his one-year term in the rotating Swiss presidency, thus heading off threats by Jewish leaders to call a boycott of Swiss banks.
He rejected the call to quit and accused the Social Democrats of using the issue to score political points at a time when relations with Jews were slowly starting to improve.
In Berne, Switzerland handed Hungary the names of 33 people, most of them Holocaust victims, whose bank accounts were declared ownerless after World War Two and credited to Budapest.

The once-secret list of names and account details, compiled by Federal Archives officials from records kept during a 1960s sweep of Swiss banks for lost Holocaust assets, aims to help the original owners or their heirs get what is rightfully theirs.
Poland got a similar list of 53 people earlier this month.
A new survey found that half the Swiss would prefer their neutral country's wartime role as a financial centre to remain a chapter of the past left to history books.

Swiss radio's poll of 1,089 people found 46 percent of people surveyed thought national authorities bore moral guilt for their anti-Jewish wartime refugee policy and business ties with the Nazis, but 51 percent wanted not to dredge up the past.
